prompt:
The GAL-TAN framework identifies political orientation on a single axis. Individuals and texts are placed according to the degree to which their views align with either pole, as follows:

  - Individuals at the GAL (Green/Alternative/Libertarian) pole support expanded
    personal freedoms and social liberalisation, for example: access to abortion,
    same-sex marriage, environmental protection, and multiculturalism.

  - Individuals at the TAN (Traditional/Authoritarian/Nationalist) pole prioritise
    order, tradition, and stability, and believe that the state should treat the
    maintenance of national identity as a priority, for example: restrictive
    immigration policy, emphasis on law and order, defence of traditional social
    institutions, and national sovereignty over supranational authority.

A text occupies a position on this axis to the extent that it argues FROM these commitments, not to the extent that it mentions the associated topics:

  - Environmental or immigration policy discussed in administrative or fiscal
    terms does not by itself indicate a position.
  - Nuclear expansion argued for energy security is not GAL.
  - Faster asylum processing argued on humanitarian grounds is not TAN.

The profile below describes the positional priorities of the British electorate.

<profile>
  tan: 0.70
  gal: 0.30
</profile>

Below are two texts.

TEXT_C:
Scottish National Party Manifesto 1997 — Summary (under 500 words)

Core vision
- “Yes We Can”: Scotland is wealthy, pays more to London than it receives, and can fund better services through independence.
- Independence is the means to deliver jobs, social justice, strong public services and a modern European democracy.

Path to independence
- A majority of SNP MPs would trigger negotiations with the UK and EU, lasting 6–12 months, followed by a single-question referendum on the settlement; then elections.
- EU membership would continue; open borders with England; pensions/investments protected by EU rules.
- Full citizenship and residence rights for all current residents.

Constitution and governance
- Written constitution and Bill of Rights, including social rights (health, housing, education, decent work).
- Unicameral Parliament elected by proportional representation; vote from age 16; public petitions; strong committees.
- Reform the monarchy’s role and funding; abolish unelected influence (no House of Lords role).
- Local government entrenched in the constitution; PR for councils.

Economy, tax and jobs
- Aim for full employment: 100,000 extra jobs; national apprenticeship scheme.
- Business tax cuts over four years: corporation tax 33p→30p; small companies 23p→18p; abolish Class IV NICs; reformed business rates.
- Growth agenda: export unit, R&D fund, tourism promotion, defence diversification.
- Fair personal taxation: introduce 15p starter rate; widen basic rate band; remove NI ceiling for higher earners; cut VAT on domestic fuel to 5%.
- Adopt EU Social Chapter; introduce a minimum wage (half median male earnings); charter for trade union rights.

Social justice and health
- Increase child benefit; restore benefits for 16–17s.
- Pensioner package: +£3/£5 per week, Cold Climate Allowance, remove standing charges for utilities, end means-testing for residential care.
- NHS: end internal market; reintegrate dentistry; +£35m p.a.; national/local health commissions; audit and prevention focus; ban tobacco advertising and raise tobacco duty.

Law, order and consumer protection
- “Zero tolerance” for community crime; bolster Procurator Fiscal service; develop alternatives to prison and rehabilitation; national vehicle register; total handgun ban; strengthen food safety via an independent Food & Consumer Health Agency.

Education, housing, local services and culture
- Hire 700 teachers; repair schools; classroom ICT and universal school internet.
- Free nursery education for all 3–4-year-olds; restore student grants; expand training; support Gaelic/Scots and community faith studies.
- Housing: transfer 75% of council housing debt to central government; build 20,000 affordable homes; renovate substandard stock; protect new/improved stock from discounted Right to Buy; abolish water quangos.
- Broadcasting: create a Scottish Broadcasting Corporation; support film via “Scottish Screen”; launch “Scot-Lot” lottery (no scratch cards).

Rural, sectoral and environment
- Abolish feudal tenure; Land Commission; transparent land register; local control of shore/seabed.
- Agriculture: BSE traceability, CAP reform, rural diversification fund; strengthen fisheries via Regional Councils, conservation, processing support.
- Forestry: double woodland in 25 years; new National Forest Enterprise Board.
- Environment: strengthen SEPA; national targets; end nuclear reprocessing at Dounreay; shift to decommissioning/renewables; phase out nuclear power; invest in renewables and conservation; ensure fair gas network access.

Transport and telecoms
- Integrate transport; bring Scottish Railtrack assets into public ownership; electrify key lines; integrate bus/rail.
- Remove Skye Bridge tolls (move to shadow tolls, then public ownership); support ferries; adjust/abolish Air Passenger Duty in H&I; improve air links.
- Expand telecoms competition and rural connectivity; back distance learning and internet adoption.

Europe, world and defence
- Full EU membership with voting rights, more MEPs, and rotating presidency.
- Targeted diplomatic network; join UN, Commonwealth, Council of Europe; British Isles association.
- Scottish Defence Forces (army, navy, air force); remove Trident; phased withdrawal from NATO due to nuclear stance; peacekeeping college; defence diversification.

Finances
- Four-year, fully costed budget; claim of large relative fiscal surplus versus UK; inherit ~£38bn debt, with £6.6bn repayment in first four years.
- Redirect spending from Trident to services; fund tax cuts, investment, and social programmes while reducing debt.

TEXT_F:
Conservative Party Manifesto 1997 — Summary (≤500 words)

Overview
The Conservatives present themselves as guardians of Britain’s economic revival since 1979 and argue for continuity: low taxes, limited government, pro-enterprise reform, constitutional stability, and a strong, sovereign UK in a flexible Europe. They contrast this with what they describe as Labour’s higher-cost “social model.”

Economy and Jobs
- Keep public spending growing more slowly than the economy; aim for government spending under 40% of GDP, move toward a balanced budget by 2000.
- Target a 20p basic income tax rate and retain a 40p top rate; keep Britain as the lowest-tax major European economy.
- Maintain 2.5% inflation target; protect low mortgage rates.
- Oppose the EU Social Chapter, Working Time Directive application to the UK, and a national minimum wage.
- Cut burdens on business, expand deregulation with “sunset” clauses, reform business rates to favor small firms, and further reduce capital gains and inheritance taxes when prudent.
- Expand welfare-to-work: extend Project Work nationally for long-term unemployed; create “Britain Works” partnerships.

Ownership, Families, Welfare
- Transfer unused personal tax allowance to a working spouse for families with dependent children/relatives (worth up to £17.50/week).
- Promote saving and share ownership (Share Match for employees); continue raising inheritance tax thresholds pragmatically.
- Pensions: introduce personal pension funds for new entrants to the workforce via NI rebates, guaranteed at least the current basic state pension; older workers unaffected.
- Social services reform for greater accountability, standards across sectors, more choice (vouchers/direct payments), respite care for carers, and a partnership model for long-term elderly care.
- Protect Child Benefit and Family Credit; intensify anti-fraud measures.

Education
- “Education Guarantee”: rigorous testing (ages 5, 7, 11, 14; publish results), tougher standards in literacy/numeracy, stricter exams, strong inspections, intervention in failing schools/LEAs, teacher appraisal tied to pupil outcomes, strengthened discipline and RE.
- Choice/diversity: more specialist schools, selective admissions by aptitude, support grammar schools where parents want them, expand Assisted Places, maintain nursery vouchers for all 4-year-olds.
- Post-16: learning credits (14–21), National Traineeships, expand Modern Apprenticeships; uphold world-class university research pending Dearing.

Health and Public Services
- NHS: real-terms increases each year; shorter waits; expand GP fundholding and primary care services (including nurse prescribing); invest via Private Finance Initiative (PFI); strengthen mental health care; prevention through “Health of the Nation.”
- Public services: extend Citizens’ Charter; expand PFI; continue privatisation and competition (complete rail, privatise London Underground and National Air Traffic Services; reform Post Office/Royal Mail while protecting universal service).

Law and Order
- More police recruitment; expand CCTV (10,000 cameras target); voluntary ID card via photo driving licence.
- Juvenile crime: parental control orders, reparation, curfews with electronic monitoring, secure training for persistent offenders.
- National Crime Squad; mandatory minimum sentences (repeat serious violent/sexual offences = automatic life; persistent burglars = 3 years; hard drug dealers = 7 years); end automatic early release; stronger victim protections.
- Legal aid within cash limits; faster criminal justice.

Society, Places, Environment
- Regenerate worst estates via tenant-led stock transfer/private capital (~£25bn over a decade); extend Rough Sleepers Initiative nationally; protect green belt; target 60% of new homes on brownfield; support rural services and jobs; no general right to roam.
- Agriculture/fisheries: robust BSE response; independent food safety leadership; CAP reform; defend quotas/limits; raise animal welfare standards EU-wide.
- Lead on environment (air/water quality, “polluter pays”).
- Expand arts, sport, and youth talent via National Lottery.

Europe, Foreign Policy, Defence, Constitution
- Europe: partnership of nation states; retain veto, rebate, border controls; oppose federalism and Social Chapter; push enlargement and single market reform.
- Single currency: keep options open; unlikely by 1999; any UK entry only after a referendum.
- Defence: stable funding, rapid deployment capability, NATO central; no defence review.
- Constitution: evolutionary reform, more open government and better Parliamentary scrutiny; oppose PR, a new Bill of Rights, and devolution to Scottish/Welsh assemblies; uphold the Union; negotiate for peace in Northern Ireland under consent principle.
